activities.caption: pair each arguer with their structure
activities.name: logicArguersMatch

config.prompt: Arguments everywhere — pair each arguer with their structure:

pairs.left: a doctor who orders a test
pairs.right: "the symptom pattern is consistent with X, the test distinguishes X, therefore test"
from load tables to girder thickness
argues from fingerprints to a suspect
a vocabulary for saying precisely why one structure works and another collapses

config.why: Arguments are everywhere and quarrels are the least interesting place they appear — extraction is the logician's job.

activities.anchor: Sherlock Holmes, despite his catchphrase, almost never deduces
activities.caption: bet on what Holmes actually does
activities.name: logicHolmesPredict

config.q: Sherlock Holmes announces that he has deduced the criminal from the clues. What has he actually done?
choices: Deduction — the conclusion was already contained in his premises
Abduction — inferred the best explanation of the effects before him
config.why: Deduction cannot introduce new facts; Holmes works from effects back to the best explanation — and so do medicine, debugging and the historical sciences.

activities.anchor: there are exactly two ways an argument can fail
activities.caption: drag the divider — the two verdicts
activities.name: logicValidCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — the two verdicts:

before.label: Validity — the shape
before.text: Could all the premises be true while the conclusion is false? If not, the shape holds — regardless of whether the premises actually are true.

after.label: Soundness — shape plus truth
after.text: Validity plus true premises. Exactly two ways to fail — a false premise, or a leaking shape — diagnosed by entirely different methods.

config.why: Validity is a promise about transmission, not origin: feed a valid shape false premises and it delivers a false conclusion with perfect efficiency.

activities.anchor: Case law is built on them
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a gloss on analogy
activities.name: logicAnalogySpot

config.prompt: One line of this gloss on analogy is wrong — click it:
lines: Analogies claim that likeness in some respects implies likeness in the respect at issue.
Two calculators from the same factory will likely share a failure rate — "same factory" is relevant to defects.
Two books from the same publisher will likewise share manufacturing defects — "same publisher" is relevant too.
What matters is whether the shared properties are relevant to the target property.
Most bad analogies fail on relevance, not on number of similarities.
config.correction: "Same publisher" is not relevant to manufacturing defects — the books share a brand, not a production line. Relevance, not similarity count, decides.
config.why: Case law and much moral reasoning are built on analogy — and the standard test is to look for a disanalogy that breaks the bridge.

activities.anchor: Modus tollens is how hypotheses die
activities.caption: walk the conditional moves, valid and invalid
activities.name: logicConditionalSteps

steps.math: Modus ponens: P → Q; P; ∴ Q

steps.note: Always valid — how hypotheses die: derive a testable consequence, show it false, and the hypothesis goes with it.

steps.math: Affirming the consequent: P → Q; Q; ∴ P
steps.note: Invalid — a sprinkler explains the wet ground too.
Invalid — the same sprinkler refutes it.
When several hypotheses survive, prefer the one that posits fewer new kinds of thing — a preference, not a proof; nature is sometimes baroque.

activities.anchor: These four are the formal fallacies: failures of
activities.caption: audit a wet-ground argument
activities.name: logicFallacyBranch

config.root: A formal audit. Someone argues: "If rain, wet ground. The ground is wet. Therefore it rained."

choices.label: Valid — rain is the obvious cause of wet ground
choices.feedback: Wet ground follows from rain, but not from rain alone — the shape leaks.

choices.label: Invalid — another cause could wet the ground
choices.feedback: Affirming the consequent — one of the two invalid mirror images of the valid conditional moves.

leak.text: The content is plausible and the shape still fails — which is exactly what a formal fallacy is: a failure of shape, not of facts.

impostor.text: Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent — versus modus ponens and modus tollens, which are always valid.

config.why: Formal fallacies are failures of shape; informal ones — ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma — fail on content.
